LETTER OF SUBMITTAL. 


DEPARTMENT OF COMMERCE AND LABOR, 
BuREAU OF STATISTICs, 
Washington, October 8, 1909. 


Sir: I have the honor to submit herewith the first three parts of 
a statistical abstract of the principal countries and colonies of the world. 
In the first part an attempt is made to show the growth of foreign 
commerce for as extensive a period as can be covered by the published 
official records of the respective countries. In some cases—as, for 
instance, the United Kingdom and France—the figures fairly cover 
the trade development of the nineteenth century; for other countries, 
such as Italy, the Balkan States, Australia, etc., these figures become 
available only since the date at which national consolidation or inde- 
pendence enabled the statistical authorities to present the figures for 
their respective countries as a whole. It has not been thought prac- 
ticable to present the earlier trade figures for those several geograph- 
ical units which in later years came to constitute the present national 
states or territorial divisions. Such figures, even if available, would 
after all have but an historical interest, and, in some cases, if used 
for comparative purposes, would prove misleading by reason of una- 
voidable duplications. 

Wherever possible, the movements of merchandise and precious 
metals have been stated separately, and under the latter head gold 
and silver also stated separately. Such a differentiation, although 
entailing considerable work—as in many cases the figures illustrating 
gold and silver movements had to be gleaned from the annual trade 
reports—was thought, however, to be justified in view of the purpose 
of the chapter to give a comprehensive view of the world’s commercial 
movements. 

While normally the specie and bullion movements may be said 
to correspond to and even partly depend on the merchandise move- 
ments, still the multiplicity of factors modifying the normal move- 
ment, such as specie loans made abroad by the national govern- 
ments or the great national banks, cash investments in foreign 
countries and the colonies, war contributions, and the like, seem to 
warrant the separate presentation of the movement of the precious 
metals. In view of the partial demonetization of silver undertaken 
by the leading commercial countries during the more recent period, it 
was thought advisable to treat the gold movement separately from 
the silver movement. The figures of specie movements are naturally 
less complete than those of merchandise movements, as they do not 
include the by no means inconsiderable amounts of specie (gold 
mainly) imported or exported by travelers, which amounts are, as a 
rule, unknown to the fiscal authorities and never made the subject of 


statistical record. : 


8 LETTER OF SUBMITTAL. 


GENERAL AND SPECIAL TRADE. 


For the more imporant countries the imports and exports of 
merchandise appear under the twofold head of ‘‘General trade” 
and “Special trade.”” The transit trade, as affecting but little the 
immediate trade relations between the countries, has, whenever ~ 
practicable, been omitted. In the case of some important countries, 
however, the term “General trade” includes the transit and trans- 
shipment trade. These countries are: Belgium, France, Italy, Ger- 
many (up to and including 1879), the Netherlands (up to and 
including 1871), and Portugal. 

In the trade accounts of most countries the term ‘‘General im- 
ports” includes all imports except those which, being intended 
for other countries, pass directly through the country—the so-called 
“transit trade”—or are merely transshipped at the port of arrival. 

The term ‘‘Special imports” includes imports of articles which 
pass directly into the hands of the consignee (both free and duti- 
able) and those which are withdrawn from warehouse on payment 
of duty. 

The term ‘‘General exports” applies to all articles which are 
sent out of the country, no matter whether they are of domestic 
or foreign origin. As a rule it does not, however, include the value 
of foreign goods merely transshipped outward at the ports of the 
country or leaving the country in transit. 

The term ‘‘Special exports” comprises the exports of articles of 
domestic production. Articles of foreign origin, which leave the 
country after being changed in form or enhanced in value by further 
manufacture in the country, are also placed in this class. Colonial 
products and other duty-free articles, such as foodstuffs and raw 
materials, in some countries, figure under this head, even though 
the ultimate foreign destination of such articles may be known at 
the time they are delivered to the consignee in the country where 
they are first landed. 

In the case of the less important countries the twofold classifica- 
tion of trade could not be given, and the figures of imports and 
exports appear as a rule under the general head of ‘‘Total trade” 
or ‘‘Merchandise;’ the latter in case the movement of precious 
metals is treated separately. 

The figures of ‘‘net imports” have been calculated for a number of 
countries (particularly the United Kingdom) for which figures of 
‘special imports” or “‘imports for consumption”’ are not available. 
This was done chiefly to facilitate international comparisons. These 
figures are arrived at by deducting from the general imports the 
figures of foreign exports, and approximately, though not quite 
accurately, represent the value of merchandise retained for home 
consumption. 

VALUATIONS. 


The values of imports and exports in the principal commercial 
countries of continental Europe are calculated-with the cooperation 
of a commission made up of official experts and representatives of 
the principal industries, who determine the average unit values for 
the past year. The total values for a certain class of articles are 
then arrived at by multiplying the total quantity by the unit value as 
laid down by the commission. This system prevails now in Germany, 
France, Italy, Austria-Hungary, and Belgium. 


_LETTER OF SUBMITTAL. 9 


For the more important articles the German commission adopts 
various unit values according to the country from which imported 
or to which exported. Since 1906 declared values have been used 
for a number of other articles. 

The other system, used by the United Kingdom and the United 
States, is based upon declarations made by the importer or exporter. 
Switzerland, while having a commission to determine the import 
values, uses the second system in determining the value of its exports. 
Without going into the technical question of correct methods of valu- 
ations, it may be stated in this connection that the British authori- 
‘ties take the value of imports to represent the cost in the country 
where purchased, plus insurance and freight, or when goods are con- 
signed for sale, the latest sale value of the goods; whereas the United 
States authorities, until the enactment of the 1909 tariff, in ascer- 
taining the values of imported articles for fiscal purposes, took 
“‘the actual market values or wholesale prices of such merchan- 
dise as bought and sold in usual wholesale quantities at the time of 
exportation to the United States in the principal markets of the coun- 
try from whence imported, and in the condition in which such mer- 
chandise is there bought for exportation to the United States or 
consigned to the United States for sale, including the value * * * 
of coverings of any kind, and all other costs, charges, and expenses 
incident to placing the merchandise in condition ready for shipment 
to the United States.”” In the case of exports the British authorities 
base the valuation on ‘‘free on board”’ values, i. e., they include besides 
the cost of the article the charge of delivering the goods on board the 
ship. The United States authorities take the value of domestic exports 
to be that prevailing at the time of exportation in the ports of the 
United States whence they are exported ; in the case of foreign exports a 
distinction is made between goods shipped ‘‘from warehouse”’ and ‘‘not 
from warehouse,” the value in the first case being the import value of the 
goods in question, and in the second case their value at the port of ship- 
ment. The European fiscal authorities in determining import and 
export values, as a rule, include the freight and other incidental costs of 
the goods to the point where the article crosses the national frontier. 
For purposes of international comparison, this fact of different systems 
and modes of valuation should always be borne in mind. From the 
American standpoint the value of imports as stated by European 
countries is too high, while from the European standpoint the value 
of the imports as stated by the United States authorities is too low. 

For the early periods the discretion of the customs authorities in fixing 
the values was extremely limited, as the customs regulations provided 
for unit values of the more important articles of imports and exports. 
Thus, for the United Kingdom, these unit values remained unchanged 
during the eighteenth century ever since 1698, when the trade statistics 
of that country were organized. It was only in 1798, when special con- 
voy (mainly ad valorem) duties began to be levied upon all imports 
and exports, that large discrepancies were found to exist between the 
real values of the exports mid the official values calculated in accord- 
ance with the provisions of the act of 1698. In 1805 the exports of 
British produce and manufactures began to be compiled upon the 
basis of the real or declared values of the ieaken tix, though in 
the case of imports the registration of real values was not begun until 
1854. The figures showing the trade of the United Kingdom reflect 
this change of method of valuation in the tables of general exports. 


10 LETTER OF SUBMITTAL. 


In France the values for 1815 to 1824, inclusive, are those fixed 
by the official commission of 1820-21. The values for 1825 to 1846 
are based upon values fixed in 1826. It was only in 1847 that the 
present system of annual values for each class of articles was adopted 
and made the basis of total valuations. The change of system is 
reflected in the figures of imports and exports. 

Practically all South American countries still maintain the old 
system of official (legal) unit values, though these values are subject 
to frequent, in some cases annual, revision. Of the European coun- 
tries the Netherlands is now the only one which still maintains the 
early system of official values for most of its imports and exports. 
As a consequence the official figures have to be used with great care, 
as some of the items are valued at prices which have remained 
unchanged since 1862 and in no way correspond to current prices of 
the articles. These and similar considerations should be borne in 
mind when an attempt is made to analyze the growth of commerce 
of the leading commercial countries. 


REDUCTION OF ORIGINAL VALUES. 


All values are stated in terms of United States currency. In the 
case of the gold-standard countries, i. e., the European countries, 
except Russia and Austria for the greater part of the period, and most 
of the European colonies, for which figures are given in the following 
tables, the rates of conversion used were those given by the United 
States Director of the Mint. The rates for the Russian credit ruble, 
in terms of which the original values are stated for the greater part 
of the period, are based upon valuations published by the Russian 
authorities. For Austria-Hungary the value of the gulden up to the 
year 1872 was calculated at the rate of 48.665 cents, equal to 2 shil- 
lings; beginning with 1873 the original values were reduced on the 
basis of estimates made by the Director of the Mint for the silver 
gulden, and for the years 1891 to 1895, inclusive, at rates kindly fur- 
nished by the Austrian authorities. For the other silver-standard 
countries the valuations of the United States Director of the Mint 
were used. Exchange rates proper were as a rule disregarded, except 
that in the case of countries on a paper-currency basis, such as Brazil 
and several other American countries, these rates were used as a 
basis for converting the original values. 


COUNTRY OF ORIGIN AND DESTINATION. 


The second: part of the abstract presents the imports and exports 
by countries of origin and destination. In the trade accounts of 
the leading countries, as a rule, goods brought into the country are 
not traced back tothe country where they were produced, nor do these 
accounts state in the case of exports the ultimate destination of the 
articles, 1. e., the country where the goods are consumed. The general 
practice designates as the country of origin that country where the 
goods were purchased and which appears in the invoice or bill of lading. 
Similarly, the country to which, according to the declaration of the 
exporter, the goods are shipped is regarded as the country of des- 
tination. Wherever proof of the origin of goods or of the country 
of original shipment is wanting, the goods are necessarily credited to 
the country of the last transshipment or to the contiguous country 
through which imported. Similarly, in the case of exports, goods are 


LETTER OF SUBMITTAL. 11 


often credited to the country where the transshipment takes place 
or to the contiguous country through whose territory the goods are 

assing. 
3 In the trade accounts of the United Kingdom prior to 1904 imports 
. were credited generally to the country whence they were shipped 
direct to the United Kingdom. Although efforts were made to trace 
the more important imports back to the actual countries of first ship- 
ment, yet in the absence of “certificates of origin” of imported 
goods this was not always possible. As a result, countries such as 
Switzerland and Bolivia, which have no seaboard, did not figure in 
the returns at all, merchandise imported from these States being 
credited to the country containing the port of last shipment. The 
same practice was followed in the case of exports, which were charged 
to the country in which the port of first discharge is situated. In the 
case of shipments originating in Russia, Germany, Austria, Italy, and 
the West Indies, which reach the United Kingdom by way of ports 
outside the country of original shipment, the imports were credited 
by the British authorities, as a rule, to the country in which the port 
of last shipment is located. Since 1904, however, separate statements 
have been published by the British authorities regarding the actual 
countries from which goods imported into the United Kingdom were 
consigned, and regarding the countries to which exported goods were 
consigned. Exports from the United States to countries having no 
direct steamship connections with American ports also appear under- 
stated in the United States accounts, whereas exports to countries 
containing the respective ports of discharge whence the goods are for- 
warded, either by land or water, to the ultimate country of destination 
as a rule are overstated. Thus the exports from the United States 
to Austria-Hungary, Russia, and Switzerland are understated, while 
those to the United Kingdom and Germany are overstated in the 
United States accounts. Generally a more correct idea of the trade 
relations between two countries can be obtained from a study of 
their respective import figures than from their export figures. 

Another source of statistical inaccuracy under this head is the fact 
that in some cases, especially of exports of staple articles, such as 
coal, cotton, sugar, etc., the ultimate destination of the goods ex- 
ported is not known at the time of shipment. Such goods appear in 
the trade accounts either with destination marked ‘‘Unknown”’ or 
else “‘Shipped for orders.’’ The value of articles thus shipped con- 
stitutes over one-third of the entire exports from Argentina and is 
also quite considerable in the case of goods exported from the Dutch 
East Indies. | 

The figures presented in the second part, so far as the European 
countries are concerned, relate to the merchandise movement only. 
In the case of most extra-European countries it has been found im- 
possible to show the same movement, and their figures of imports and 
exports by countries of origin and destination include the move- 
ment of the precious metals. Wherever the figures relate to total 
trade, including the movement of gold and silver, the fact is noted in 
footnotes to the tables. 


IMPORTS AND EXPORTS BY ARTICLES. 


The third part of the abstract presents the trade of the leading 
countries and colonies by principal classes of articles. ‘These articles 
have been grouped more or less uniformly in accordance with the clas- 


12 LETTER OF SUBMITTAL. 


sification adopted in the trade accounts of the United States. This 
involved the complete rearrangement of the trade figures of most coun- 
tries. The new arrangement is not supposed to meet the oft- 
expressed desire for a uniform classification of the imports and exports 
of all countries. The aim has been merely to arrange the forei 
material in a manner which experience has proved to be most suit- 
able to the requirements of the business interests of this country and 
which may therefore facilitate the use of this volume by the persons 
who are most likely to consult it. It is hoped that the new abstract 
dealing with commercial and industrial conditions in foreign countries 
may thus become in time a companion volume to the Statistical 
Abstract of the United States. In order to increase the practical 
usefulness of the new publication, all foreign weights, measures, and 
currency have been expressed in terms of United States equivalents. 
Items likely to be of interest to the American importer or exporter 
have been specified even when they happen to be only of secondary 
importance in the trade accounts of the foreign countries. 

The figures in the second and third parts cover, as a rule, the 
special trade movements for the period 1896 to 1906. Only for the 

nited Kingdom are reexports of foreign and colonial merchandise 
stated in addition to the domestic exports. 


SUBSEQUENT CHAPTERS OF THE ABSTRACT. 


The Bureau has.in preparation further parts of the abstract, deal- 
ing with the area and the growth of population of the principal coun- 
tries, and the production of the leading staples, including the principal 
agricultural and mineral products. Another part contemplated will 
contain the principal navigation statistics for the leading countries 
and ports. Itis also proposed to present the principal data regard- 
ing the public revenues and expenditures, the growth of public debts, 
the principal monetary and banking statistics, etc. In future issues 
of the abstract statistics will be given also regarding the growth of 
railways, telegraphs, and other means of communication. 

The preparation of this work, under the general direction of the 
Chief of the Bureau of Statistics, has been in immediate charge of 
Mr. Morris Jacobson, of this Bureau, whose familiarity with the 
statistical methods and official publications of the various foreign 
countries, and the languages in which they are published, has enabled 
him to direct intelligently the work of the corps of experts engaged 
in translating the statements of the various official documents from 
which the information was obtained, and transforming their state- 
ments of quantities and values into terms familiar to the people of 
the United States, for whose especial information this volume has 
been prepared. This work of transforming commercial statistics 
expressed in the language, currency, weights, and measures of the 
various foreign countries to which these statistics relate has been 
one requiring painstaking care and attention, and has occupied for 
several years the time of the limited force which the Bureau was 
able to assign to this important task. 

Respectfully, O. P. Austin, 
Chief of Bureau. 
To Hon. Cuaries NAGEL, 
Secretary of Commerce and Labor.
